documents.title: Establishing Expectations: Syllabus Language and Policies for Generative AI Use
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule itself: it says 'these are not official MSU policies' and offers four tiers and sample statements as 'starting points' for each course, so the decision is delegated to instructors.
documents.summary: Teaching-center page telling instructors to set AI expectations in the syllabus. It lists four levels of use and gives sample syllabus statements for allowing, prohibiting and requiring AI, plus citation advice.

units.why: Instructors are told they 'should set expectations' in the syllabus, class and assignments, so this is a syllabus-statement duty addressed to instructors at course start; P09 fits because it covers stating AI expectations in the syllabus.
units.anchor: Instructors should set expectations for students in the syllabus
units.frag_end: generative AI can be used from the beginning.

units.why: The page offers four named levels ('not allowed', 'allowed with attribution', 'limited', 'encouraged or required') as examples; naming tiers of use matches P05.
units.anchor: Four examples for content-generating AI could be:
units.policy: The center offers four example levels of AI use for content-generating AI: not allowed, allowed with appropriate attribution, allowed in limited instances, and encouraged broadly or required.

units.why: This tier says 'It's not allowed' and accepts only student or group content, a default ban on AI-produced work (P01) rather than the generic tier list in P05.
units.anchor: Only content done by a student or as part of an assigned group is accepted.

units.why: This tier allows AI-assisted work 'when students clearly identify what parts' were AI generated, so the core rule is disclosure with each submission (P24) rather than the permissive default P02.
units.anchor: allowed when students clearly identify what parts of the assignment were AI generated
units.policy: AI-assisted work on some assignments is allowed when students clearly identify what parts of the assignment were AI generated and how it helped them.

units.why: This tier allows AI 'to prepare for assignments by brainstorming' with students showing how it helped; brainstorming (P15) is the specific permitted use, while the showing requirement is secondary.
units.anchor: AI can be used to prepare for assignments by brainstorming
units.policy: AI can be used to prepare for assignments by brainstorming, but students must show how it helped them reach the result.

units.why: This tier says 'Use is encouraged broadly or required' with students identifying AI-generated parts; it is the default permit/encourage option (P02).
units.anchor: Use is encouraged broadly or required: Students can use AI but must identify

units.why: The page states 'these are not official MSU policies' and are starting points for individual courses, so the university guidance leaves the rule to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: these are not official MSU policies around generative AI use
units.policy: The example syllabus statements are not official MSU policies and are guides for faculty to create policies and expectations for their individual courses.

units.why: The example 'allowing' statement says 'you may utilize AI language models, including ChatGPT' for writing assignments, a prose-specific permission (P18).
units.anchor: you may utilize AI language models, including ChatGPT, as a resource
units.frag_start: In this course, you may utilize
units.policy: In this example course, students may utilize AI language models, including ChatGPT, as a resource to support their writing assignments.

units.why: The sample statement says AI is 'not a substitute for your critical thinking and creativity' and should be a supplement; students stay the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: not a substitute for your critical thinking and creativity
units.policy: In the example statement, AI is not a substitute for the student's critical thinking and creativity; students apply it as a supplement to the writing process and do not rely solely on its suggestions.

units.why: 'Ultimately, you are responsible for the content and quality' makes students own their submission (P29).
units.anchor: you are responsible for the content and quality of your written assignment

units.why: The statement says students 'should critically evaluate ChatGPT outputs for accuracy, potential bias, and relevancy', a verification duty (P31).
units.anchor: you should critically evaluate ChatGPT outputs for accuracy, potential bias, and relevancy

units.why: The statement requires writing to be 'original and properly attributed, including citing outputs', a disclosure/citation duty (P24); the APA reference is detail beyond P25.
units.anchor: ensure that your writing remains original and properly attributed, including citing outputs
units.policy: Students ensure their writing remains original and properly attributed, including citing outputs or text generated by ChatGPT.

units.why: 'I encourage you to use AI language models' to enhance writing skills is an explicit encouragement, matching P02 (default encourage).
units.anchor: I encourage you to use AI language models to enhance your writing skills

units.why: Students with questions are told to 'discuss them with me', inviting questions to the instructor about AI use; P10 covers asking the instructor.
units.anchor: please discuss them with me.
units.policy: Students with questions or concerns about using AI language models for writing assignments discuss them with the instructor.

units.why: The prohibiting statement says 'I have decided to prohibit the use of ChatGPT or similar tools', a course-wide ban (P01).
units.anchor: I have decided to prohibit the use of ChatGPT or similar tools during this course

units.why: The statement explains that relying on AI 'undermines the learning objectives' because students should develop independent thinking; this is the practice-builds-skill rationale (P41).
units.anchor: relying on them for this course undermines the learning objectives
units.policy: The example prohibition says relying on AI language models undermines the learning objectives, since students are to develop skills in independent thinking, problem-solving, and engagement with the subject matter.

units.why: The ban 'applies to all aspects of the course, including assignments, exams' so it reaches exams, matching P22 rather than only P01.
units.anchor: this requirement applies to all aspects of the course, including assignments, exams
units.policy: In the example prohibition, the ban applies to all aspects of the course, including assignments, exams, and any form of communication related to the course content.

units.why: 'Any use ... will be considered a violation student code of conduct' classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: will be considered a violation student code of conduct
units.frag_start: Any use of AI language models

units.why: The requiring statement says 'I have decided to make the use of ChatGPT a requirement throughout this course', which builds AI into the course (P02 expect).
units.anchor: I have decided to make the use of ChatGPT a requirement throughout this course

units.why: MSU 'seek[s] to empower you with the necessary skills' for technology, a skill and career-readiness rationale (P44).
units.anchor: we seek to empower you with the necessary skills to navigate and leverage these advancements
units.policy: The example requirement says MSU seeks to empower students with the necessary skills to navigate and leverage technological advancements effectively.

units.why: The requirement 'applies to all aspects of the course, including assignments, exams', and AI use 'will contribute to your overall evaluation', so AI is built into assessment (P02 over P22 because it requires rather than bans).
units.anchor: Applying AI language models, including ChatGPT, will be an integral part
units.frag_start: this requirement applies to all aspects
units.policy: In the example requirement, applying AI language models, including ChatGPT, is an integral part of the learning process and contributes to the overall evaluation and assessment in the course.

units.why: The instructor commits to 'provide guidance, resources, and assistance' to help students use ChatGPT, a support commitment attached to a required tool; no sanctioned tool is provided so P17 does not fit and no other type does.
units.anchor: I will provide guidance, resources, and assistance
units.frag_end: within the framework of this course.
units.policy: In the example requirement, the instructor will provide guidance, resources, and assistance to help students effectively utilize ChatGPT.
units.uncovered_note: Instructor commits to support and guidance for students when AI use is required; no sanctioned tool is provided so P17 does not fit.

units.why: The guidance suggests initially discussing responsible use with students, giving them agency; this co-creation of expectations fits no type exactly (not a syllabus statement), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: engage students in an initial discussion around the responsible use of generative AI
units.policy: Instructors can partner with and engage students in an initial discussion around the responsible use of generative AI, which promotes transparency and gives students some agency.
units.uncovered_note: Co-creating AI expectations with students through an initial class discussion.

units.why: The page says the discussion can point out 'inaccurate information and/or biased content that students could be accountable for', a verify-output warning (P31).
units.anchor: inaccurate information and/or biased content that students could be accountable for
units.policy: The discussion can point out Open AI's limitations, including issues with inaccurate information and/or biased content that students could be accountable for.

units.why: The BU example 'requires students to show how and give credit to AI tools', a disclosure rule (P24) cited as a model.
units.anchor: requires students to show how and give credit to AI tools when they are used
units.policy: The cited Boston University policy requires students to show how and give credit to AI tools when they are used.

units.why: The BU example states how instructors will 'assess and possibly penalize merely reproducing AI output', i.e. reproducing AI output is not acceptable (P19); the penalty is not concrete enough for P37.
units.anchor: possibly penalize merely reproducing AI output use by students
units.frag_start: expectations for how instructors will assess
units.policy: The cited Boston University policy sets expectations for how instructors will assess and possibly penalize students merely reproducing AI output, and emphasizes using AI tools wisely to deepen understanding.

units.why: 'provide resources and teach your students how to cite their use' directs instructors who allow AI to teach citation, a disclosure requirement (P24).
units.anchor: provide resources and teach your students how to cite their use of content produced
units.frag_start: If you decide to allow limited or full use
units.policy: Instructors who allow limited or full use of generative AI provide resources and teach students how to cite their use of content produced by the tool.

documents.unit: Montana University System, Commissioner of Higher Education
documents.title: Commissioner's Directive: Generative AI Adoption and Use
documents.stance_why: The directive directs campuses to 'adopt campus-level essential practices' and 'establish clear AI use expectations for instruction' without itself allowing or banning student AI use, so it hands the decision to campuses.
documents.summary: System commissioner's directive telling campuses to engage with eight core AI principles, adopt essential practices and set clear instruction expectations. It names no student-level rule and promises system resources and updates.

units.why: The directive opens by naming 'real risks, including threats to data privacy and security, academic integrity, research reliability, and equity of access', setting the framework's rationale (P56).
units.anchor: real risks, including threats to data privacy and security, academic integrity
units.policy: The directive states that AI technologies introduce real risks, including threats to data privacy and security, academic integrity, research reliability, and equity of access.

units.why: Campuses are 'directed to' engage with the eight core principles; this is a system-level framework requirement (P56).
units.anchor: Engage with the MUS Core Principles for AI Use
units.policy: Campus CEOs and chief academic officers ensure that leadership, faculty governance bodies, and administrative units review and discuss the eight MUS core principles, which should inform campus policy, practice, and professional development.

units.why: The directive lists the eight principles including 'academic integrity' and 'restricted uses', defining the system principles (P56).
units.anchor: data privacy and security; transparency and accountability; bias awareness and mitigation; human discretion
units.policy: The eight MUS core principles are data privacy and security; transparency and accountability; bias awareness and mitigation; human discretion; protection of intellectual property; academic integrity; restricted uses; and use of approved and non-approved tools.

units.why: Each institution 'shall review' and adopt campus essential practices in institutional policy, a mandatory system framework step (P56).
units.anchor: Each MUS institution shall review the campus essential practices
units.policy: Each MUS institution shall review the campus essential practices and considerations across procurement and software, instruction, and research, and adopt them in institutional policy and operations as appropriate to institutional context, size, and capacity.

units.why: Campuses are told to give 'particular attention to establishing clear AI use expectations for instruction'; this is the closest to requiring stated expectations (P09).
units.anchor: establishing clear AI use expectations for instruction
units.policy: Campuses are expected to give particular attention to establishing clear AI use expectations for instruction.

units.why: 'risk-based procurement safeguards' for AI direct campuses to review tool purchasing, matching institutional review of AI vendor arrangements (P65).
units.anchor: risk-based procurement safeguards
units.policy: Campuses are expected to give particular attention to implementing risk-based procurement safeguards.

units.why: The directive expects campuses to be 'reinforcing research integrity standards for AI-assisted scholarship', an AI-in-research rule (P62).
units.anchor: reinforcing research integrity standards for AI-
units.policy: Campuses are expected to give particular attention to reinforcing research integrity standards for AI-assisted scholarship.

units.why: OCHE will develop 'system-wide AI literacy resources for students, faculty, and staff' and professional development, a support commitment (P63).
units.anchor: system-wide AI literacy resources for students, faculty, and staff
units.policy: OCHE will develop and make available system-wide AI literacy resources for students, faculty, and staff, including materials hosted in Canvas Commons and professional development opportunities.

units.why: OCHE will keep 'a centralized inventory of vetted AI tools' and coordinate optional access to ChatMT.ai, a sanctioned tool (P17); vetting aspect is secondary.
units.anchor: coordinating optional campus access to ChatMT.ai as a secure, cost-effective option
units.policy: OCHE will establish a centralized inventory of vetted AI tools available to campuses, including coordinating optional campus access to ChatMT.ai as a secure, cost-effective option for accessing frontier AI models.

units.why: OCHE will distribute 'sample syllabus language, AI disclosure guidance, and discipline-specific examples' to faculty, supporting syllabus statements (P09).
units.anchor: sample syllabus language, AI disclosure guidance, and discipline-specific examples
units.policy: OCHE will curate and distribute faculty-facing resources including sample syllabus language, AI disclosure guidance, and discipline-specific examples.

units.why: The guidance is called 'living guidance' that OCHE 'will update', stating a revision commitment (P54).
units.anchor: intended as living guidance. OCHE will update the document
units.frag_start: The MUS AI Task Force Recommendations are
units.policy: The MUS AI Task Force Recommendations are intended as living guidance, and OCHE will update the document as AI technologies, legal and regulatory requirements, and institutional practices continue to evolve.

units.why: Campuses 'are encouraged to treat their own AI policies ... as similarly adaptive, revisiting and revising them regularly', a regular-review recommendation (P54).
units.anchor: revisiting and revising them regularly in response to new developments
units.policy: Campuses are encouraged to treat their own AI policies and practices as adaptive, revisiting and revising them regularly in response to new developments.

units.why: 'Campus feedback ... should be submitted to OCHE' invites feedback on the guidance (P54).
units.anchor: Campus feedback on the MUS AI guidance
units.policy: Campus feedback on the MUS AI guidance, including suggested edits, emerging practices, and resource links, should be submitted to OCHE to support ongoing updates.

notes: Coder A. No school or computing-unit policy found; course layer deferred. MUS directive is a system-wide directive; it defers to campuses and contains no student-level AI rule. CFE example syllabus statements are explicitly not official MSU policy but are coded as the page presents them.
